nodes.body: Rain tapped the window. Tap, tap, tap. Milo pressed his nose to the glass. The big rain slowed to a soft drizzle. Grandma smiled. "Do you know what day this is? Puddle Jumping Day!" "Hooray!" cried Milo. He ran to get his rain things.

choices.label: Put on red rubber boots and a yellow raincoat.

nodes.body: Milo pulled on his red boots. He pushed his arms into the yellow raincoat. Zip! Grandma opened the front door. The world was drippy and shiny. It smelled like wet leaves. The sidewalk sparkled, as if it had waited just for Milo.

By the garden gate sat the first puddle. It was round like a cookie. Milo did one warm-up hop. Splish! The water jumped too. "Good hop," laughed Grandma. She took his hand, and they walked down to the corner.

At the corner the walk went two ways. One way was the tree lane. The trees dripped, and small puddles dotted the path like polka dots. The other way was the hill, where rain water raced down the curb and chattered. "You pick," said Grandma.

choices.label: Take the quiet, dripping tree lane.
Take the hill with its chattering stream.

nodes.body: Under the trees, drops fell on Milo's hood. Plip. Plop. He hopped from puddle to puddle down the polka-dot lane. Then he stopped. Something on the wet path was wiggling, small and slow, right by his boot. "Grandma, look!" he whispered.

choices.label: Look closer at a tiny wiggle.

nodes.body: It was a little earthworm. It wiggled on the hard wet path, far from any soft dirt. Just past it shone a huge puddle, flat as a mirror. "What shall we do?" asked Grandma. "Help the worm home? Or go look in that big puddle?"

choices.label: Tiptoe to the huge, mirror-flat puddle.

nodes.body: Milo found a big wet leaf. Grandma helped him scoot the worm on, gentle as a feather. It was a tiny stretcher. Step. Step. Step. They carried the worm to the soft brown dirt of the flower bed.

choices.label: Set the little earthworm down gently.

nodes.body: The worm slid into the dirt and gave one happy wiggle. Home at last. Grandma gave Milo a high five. Her wet glove went squelch. They splashed all the way home for warm cocoa, and at dinner Milo told everyone about the little worm.

The puddle was the biggest one Milo had ever seen. It held a whole upside-down sky. Milo saw clouds in it. He saw two smiling faces too, his and Grandma's. He backed up three big steps and bent his knees.

"One," said Grandma. "Two. Three!" Milo ran. His boots went thump, thump, thump. His raincoat flapped like wings. He jumped as high as he could, up over the shiny puddle. For one whole second, Milo was flying.

choices.label: Come down with a great big Splash.

nodes.body: SPLASH! Silver drops flew up like fireworks. They pattered down on two hoods. The puddle wobbled into rings, giggling all the way to the edge. Milo was soaked. Grandma was soaked. Nobody minded one bit. That was the biggest splash of the whole day.

Rain water hurried along the curb. It burbled and rushed downhill like a tiny river. A leaf sailed by like a little boat. It spun once and zoomed away. Far down the hill, the clouds opened, and one warm sunbeam poked through.

Milo trotted beside the chattering stream. Grandma picked up a wide brown leaf. "Here is a boat," she said. Down below, the sunbeam grew brighter and warmer. Milo could race the leaf boat down the stream. Or he could follow the sun down the hill.
Milo set the leaf boat on the water. Off it went! It bobbed. It twirled. It bumped past a twig and swung around a gray pebble. Milo ran along beside it. "Go, boat, go!" he cheered.

Near the bottom of the hill, the water swirled toward the drain grate. That was the finish line. The leaf boat wobbled. It tipped. Then it popped up straight and shot ahead. Milo reached out his hand.

Got it! Milo scooped up the leaf boat right at the finish line. It was drippy. He was proud. "Hooray!" cheered Grandma. Milo tucked the winning leaf into his pocket like a shiny medal. Then they stomped and splashed all the way home to tell everyone.

They followed the sunbeam down the hill. The drizzle turned to sprinkles. Then it stopped. Milo held out his hand and felt no rain at all. Every puddle turned gold, like little mirrors full of treasure. The whole street sparkled.
At the bottom of the hill, Grandma stopped. She pointed up over the rooftops. "Milo," she said softly. "Look." Milo held her hand tight. He tipped his head way back and looked up, up, up.

A rainbow! It arched all the way over the town. Its stripes glowed in the clean blue sky. "Red," said Milo. "Orange. Yellow. Green. Blue. Purple." They named every color. Then they walked home right under it, the best surprise of Puddle Jumping Day.
